provinces.name: British Columbia
provinces.analysis:
British Columbia's unemployment rate held at 6.1% in February 2026, unchanged from the prior period, while the employment rate declined to 60.5% from 60.9% and the participation rate fell to 64.4% from 64.8%.1 Provincial CPI slowed to +1.0% year-over-year from +1.3%, and housing starts registered 41,331 units, down from 41,492 in the preceding period.1,2

Finance Minister Brenda Bailey tabled BC Budget 2026 on February 17, 2026 for the 2026-27 fiscal year, describing the plan as making disciplined choices about constraining spending and raising revenue to strengthen the province's fiscal position and protect critical services.3,4 The budget allocates $400 million for the new British Columbia Strategic fund, anchored in a long-term economic strategy, alongside targeted investments in skills training, health care, child care, K-12 education, and services for children and youth.3

BC Budget 2026 identifies energy transition and competitiveness as long-term provincial economic pillars; Finance Minister Bailey also serves as Minister of Jobs, Economic Development and Innovation, and the budget's strategic fund allocations span BC's Pacific gateway commodity industries including LNG, copper, lumber, and metallurgical coal.5,6

A new urgent and primary care centre opened at UBC, expanding team-based health care access for Vancouver residents under the province's health infrastructure program.7 Two new rental buildings opened in West Vancouver under Minister of Housing Ravi Kahlon's middle-income housing program, providing additional rental supply for workers and families.8

The BC government provided $1 million to support the first BC Lions CFL regular season game series in Kelowna, connected to the province's tourism and economic development programming for the Okanagan region.9
provinces.sectorHighlights:
National construction GDP grew +0.3% month-over-month and +2.0% year-over-year, providing macro context for BC's capital activity this week.8 BC Budget 2026 allocates capital for health care infrastructure and housing programs province-wide, and two new rental buildings opened in West Vancouver as part of Housing Minister Ravi Kahlon's middle-income housing initiative — directly tied to the residential construction sector.8 BC housing starts registered 41,331 units in February 2026, a marginal decline from 41,492 units in the prior period.2

National utilities GDP rose +2.7% month-over-month. BC Budget 2026 identifies energy transition as a long-term economic pillar; natural gas is priced at $2.846/MMBtu this week, directly relevant to BC's LNG export infrastructure and provincial energy capital programs.3

National healthcare and social assistance GDP held flat month-over-month with +2.2% year-over-year growth. BC expanded team-based primary care infrastructure with the opening of a new urgent and primary care centre at UBC, adding capacity in the Greater Vancouver health corridor as part of the province's health facility investment program.7
provinces.labourDeepDive:
BC's participation rate fell to 64.4% in February 2026 from 64.8% in the prior period, while the employment rate declined to 60.5% from 60.9%.1 The unemployment rate held at 6.1%, unchanged month-over-month — the simultaneous decline in both the participation rate and the employment rate, with unemployment stable, indicates the measured labour force contracted during the period rather than shifting into unemployment.1

BC Budget 2026 includes skills training investments as a component of the province's labour strategy, addressing workforce development alongside the participation rate softness in the February data.3 Housing starts of 41,331 units in February 2026 provide a proxy indicator for construction sector employment demand; no province-specific sector-level hiring spike data was available in articles published this week.2
provinces.consumerPulse: BC Budget 2026 targets middle-income workers and families through housing capital programs, with two new rental buildings opened in West Vancouver under Minister Ravi Kahlon's initiative, adding rental supply for that income segment.8 BC's provincial CPI recorded +1.0% year-over-year inflation in February 2026, down from +1.3% in the prior period, reflecting reduced consumer price pressure across the province relative to the preceding month.1
provinces.tradeExposure:
BC's Pacific gateway position connects the province's export economy to Asia-Pacific commodity demand, with copper priced at $315.00 this week — relevant to BC mining sector project feasibility across the province's Interior and northern resource corridors.3 Natural gas at $2.846/MMBtu is the benchmark for BC's LNG export revenues, while Newcastle coal at $96.00/tonne affects BC metallurgical coal export receipts to Asian steel producers.

BC Budget 2026 identifies energy transition and Pacific competitiveness as strategic economic priorities, with the $400 million British Columbia Strategic fund positioned within the broader fiscal framework that governs provincial capital investment in commodity-linked sectors.3,4
provinces.marketContext:
The Bank of Canada's policy rate at 2.25% sets the benchmark borrowing cost for BC's construction, housing, and resource development sectors.10 The current rate level directly affects mortgage financing for residential projects, including the middle-income rental housing program delivering new supply in West Vancouver this week.8

BC's export-oriented commodity sectors — copper, LNG, lumber, and metallurgical coal — face CAD/USD exchange rate dynamics that affect competitiveness in Asia-Pacific markets; the BoC's 2.25% rate and BC Budget 2026's fiscal framework form the combined monetary-fiscal backdrop for provincial capital investment decisions.3,10

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.analysis:
Saskatchewan's unemployment rate rose to 5.6% in February 2026 from 5.3% the prior month, while the employment rate declined to 63.4% from 64.0% and the participation rate fell to 67.1% from 67.6%.1 Provincial GDP recorded +3.4% growth for 2024; national mining and oil & gas GDP contracted 0.9% month-over-month and grew 1.3% year-over-year in the latest StatCan data.2

Agriculture remained a structurally important sector for Saskatchewan, with national agricultural GDP recording a 7.6% year-over-year gain despite a 0.8% monthly decline.2 Wheat stood at $607.25 per bushel this week, with potash exports exceeding $7 billion annually and uranium production contributing to a resource-intensive export base.3

The Government of Saskatchewan tabled its 2026-27 Budget on March 18, 2026, projecting an $819 million deficit and a gradual return to balance over a five-year horizon.4 The budget includes tax measures delivering approximately $200 million in combined savings and raises the large financial institution capital tax rate to six percent from four percent.5,6 The federal and Saskatchewan governments separately announced a workforce partnership to support workers affected by tariff-related trade disruptions.7

The Saskatoon Downtown Event and Entertainment District advanced from Proposed to Under Review status under the federal Impact Assessment Act this week.8 The province also announced a $2 million investment in 2026-27 to expand its Electronic Monitoring Program by 100 additional GPS-enabled units.9
provinces.sectorHighlights:
National agriculture GDP grew 7.6% year-over-year while declining 0.8% month-over-month in the latest StatCan release.2 Saskatchewan is among Canada's largest wheat-producing provinces; wheat was priced at $607.25 per bushel this week, and potash — the province's largest single export commodity — exceeded $7 billion in annual shipments, with global fertilizer demand setting the price level.3

National mining and oil & gas GDP fell 0.9% month-over-month and gained 1.3% year-over-year.2 WTI crude oil stood at $102.18 per barrel this week, a level that supports activity in Saskatchewan's southeastern oil-producing regions.3 The federal-provincial workforce partnership targeting tariff-affected industries signals acknowledged exposure in Saskatchewan's trade-oriented resource sectors.7
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Saskatchewan's participation rate declined to 67.1% in February 2026 from 67.6% the prior month, and the employment rate fell to 63.4% from 64.0%; the unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 5.6%.1 The concurrent decline in participation and employment rates indicates net contraction in labour force attachment alongside the increase in unemployment.1

The federal-provincial workforce support partnership announced this week identifies tariff-related trade disruption as a source of labour market pressure in trade-exposed industries across the province.7 The 2026 Skills Canada Saskatchewan Provincial Competition gathered approximately 300 high school, post-secondary, and apprenticeship participants in Regina, reflecting continued provincial investment in skilled trades pipelines.10
provinces.consumerPulse: Saskatchewan's CPI turned negative at -0.7% in February 2026, down from a prior reading of +1.2%, marking a reversal in recent provincial price trends.1 The 2026-27 Budget included tax reductions projected to deliver approximately $200 million in combined consumer and business savings, while projecting provincial deficits through to the end of the decade.4,5 Housing starts reached 5,486 units in February 2026, up from 5,327 the prior month, indicating continued residential construction activity in the province.11
provinces.tradeExposure:
WTI crude oil was priced at $102.18 per barrel as of March 31, 2026, supporting activity in Saskatchewan's southeastern oil-producing areas.3 Wheat stood at $607.25 per bushel; Saskatchewan's grain export revenues track closely with global commodity price movements, and the province is among Canada's leading wheat-producing regions.3

Potash exports exceed $7 billion annually, with global fertilizer demand setting price levels for Saskatchewan's largest export commodity; uranium production adds further resource diversification to the provincial export base.12 The federal-provincial tariff-impacted worker partnership announced this week signals recognized exposure of Saskatchewan's trade-dependent industries to shifting global trade conditions.7
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026, setting the cost floor for capital financing across Saskatchewan's project pipeline.13 The Saskatoon Downtown Event and Entertainment District, which advanced to Under Review under the federal Impact Assessment Act this week, and the multi-year capital program outlined in the 2026-27 Budget both operate within this financing environment.8,4

provinces.name: Manitoba
provinces.analysis:
Manitoba's unemployment rate fell to 5.7% in February 2026 from 6.3% in the prior period, according to Statistics Canada.1 The provincial employment rate stood at 62.5%, down from 62.9%, while the participation rate was 66.3% compared to 67.1% in January 2026.1

National agriculture and forestry GDP contracted 0.8% month-over-month in the most recent period while posting a 7.6% year-over-year gain, providing macro context for Manitoba's grain and oilseed export base.5 National construction GDP grew 0.3% month-over-month and 2.0% year-over-year, a backdrop relevant to Manitoba's housing starts of 7,642 annualized units in February 2026, down from 7,799 in January 2026.2

The Manitoba NDP government released Budget 2026 on March 24, 2026, projecting total provincial spending of $27.3 billion — an increase of $1.4 billion, or approximately 5.4%, from the 2025-26 fiscal year.3 The budget eliminates provincial sales tax on all food sold in grocery stores effective July 1, 2026.3 Scotiabank Economics noted the fiscal path to balance is largely unchanged from the prior outlook, with deficit reduction contingent on federal transfer payments.4 The Canadian Innovators Coalition published commentary calling on the Manitoba government to maintain its value-added economic strategy in the context of US trade policy pressures.6

The City of Winnipeg confirmed that ultraviolet treatment at the North End Water Pollution Control Centre resumed following a maintenance outage, restoring pathogen neutralization capacity for effluent discharged near the Red River.7 The March 23, 2026 settlement payment deadline in the Winnipeg Police Service headquarters litigation passed; under a council-approved tiered settlement, the Caspian defendants were required to remit $23 million to the City.8
provinces.sectorHighlights:
Agriculture is Manitoba's primary export sector. National agriculture and forestry GDP posted a 7.6% year-over-year gain against a 0.8% month-over-month contraction in the most recent period, according to Statistics Canada.5 Spring wheat and canola are key Manitoba export commodities. The Canadian Innovators Coalition's Budget 2026 commentary identified Manitoba's value-added food and agricultural processing sector as central to the province's sovereign economic positioning amid US trade policy shifts.6

National construction GDP grew 0.3% month-over-month and 2.0% year-over-year in the latest available data.5 Manitoba housing starts totalled 7,642 annualized units in February 2026, a decline from 7,799 in January 2026, according to CMHC.2 Budget 2026 projects $27.3 billion in total provincial spending for 2026-27, with increased allocation across social and infrastructure programs; specific capital expenditure by sector was not itemized in available sources.3
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Manitoba's unemployment rate declined to 5.7% in February 2026 from 6.3% the prior month, according to Statistics Canada.1 The participation rate fell to 66.3% from 67.1%, and the employment rate moved to 62.5% from 62.9% over the same period.1 The concurrent decline in both unemployment and participation rate indicates that some individuals exited the labour force during the reference period rather than transitioning into employment.

No province-specific sector-level hiring or layoff data was available in this week's news releases. The City of Winnipeg awarded a contract to Main Street Project for 24/7 mobile outreach services covering individuals at risk of or experiencing homelessness, continuing publicly funded frontline staffing in social services.9
provinces.consumerPulse: Manitoba Budget 2026, released March 24, 2026, removes provincial sales tax from all food sold in grocery stores effective July 1, 2026.3 A Globe Newswire commentary noted the budget did not extend the food tax exemption to restaurant meals, leaving that segment taxable.10 Manitoba's provincial CPI stood at +3.1% year-over-year in February 2026, down from +3.4% in the prior period, according to Statistics Canada.1
provinces.tradeExposure: Manitoba's trade profile is agriculture-dependent, with spring wheat and canola as primary export commodities and nickel extraction centred in Thompson. Manitoba Hydro exports electricity to US Midwest markets, and CentrePort Canada's inland port in Winnipeg provides logistics connections to US supply chains. The Canadian Innovators Coalition flagged Manitoba's exposure to US trade policy developments in its Budget 2026 commentary, noting the province's value-added manufacturing and processing sectors as areas of trade policy sensitivity.6
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada policy rate stood at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026. Manitoba's $27.3 billion Budget 2026 spending plan carries provincial borrowing costs tied to prevailing Government of Canada benchmark yields.3 Manitoba housing starts of 7,642 annualized units in February 2026 represent the residential construction pipeline active in the current rate environment.2

provinces.name: Newfoundland & Labrador
provinces.analysis:
Province-specific GDP and labour market indicators for Newfoundland & Labrador are pending release from Statistics Canada and will be updated via primary API feeds upon publication. The Bank of Canada holds its policy rate at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026, with offshore resource development and fisheries activity remaining central to provincial economic conditions this week.1

Premier Wakeham and the Minister of Energy and Mines attended CERAWeek 2026 to represent Newfoundland and Labrador's offshore energy sector. WTI crude is priced at $102.18/bbl. The province's three active offshore production facilities — Hibernia, Hebron, and Terra Nova — constitute the primary driver of provincial resource royalties and export revenues.2

The federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans set the 2026 Total Allowable Catch for the Newfoundland and Labrador snow crab fishery at 61,004 tonnes, a 3% decrease from the 2025 level. DFO simultaneously launched a Precautionary Approach Review for the fishery, signalling a structured reassessment of harvest sustainability.3

The Government of Newfoundland and Labrador advanced legislation in the House of Assembly on March 30 to make permanent the reduction in the provincial gas tax on gasoline and diesel. Budget 2026 public consultations have gathered input on healthcare, lower taxes, and safer communities as the government's stated platform priorities.4

The Provincial Government and the Newfoundland and Labrador Dental Association reached a tentative agreement covering the Children's Dental Program, Adult Dental Program, and Surgical Dental Program. Minister of Forestry, Agriculture and Lands Forsey was scheduled to participate in a Wildfire Preparedness and Resilience Partner Forum on March 31, hosted by Newfoundland Power at Pippy Park.5
provinces.sectorHighlights:
National Mining/Oil & Gas GDP contracted M/M -0.9% but expanded Y/Y +1.3%. In Newfoundland & Labrador, Premier Wakeham attended CERAWeek 2026 to promote the province's offshore energy assets. WTI crude is at $102.18/bbl, above the production economics threshold for the Hibernia, Hebron, and Terra Nova offshore fields, which drive provincial royalty revenues.2

The federal government announced the 2026 snow crab TAC at 61,004 tonnes, down 3% from 2025, along with the launch of a Precautionary Approach Review for the Newfoundland and Labrador fishery. National Agriculture and Forestry GDP registered M/M -0.8% but Y/Y +7.6%.3

National Construction GDP grew M/M +0.3% and Y/Y +2.0%. Minister Forsey participated in a Wildfire Preparedness and Resilience Partner Forum hosted by Newfoundland Power on March 31, addressing forestry and land resilience planning across the province.6

provinces.consumerPulse: The Government of Newfoundland and Labrador advanced legislation on March 30 to make the provincial gas tax reduction on gasoline and diesel permanent, directly affecting fuel costs for households and commercial operators across the province.4 Budget 2026 public consultations focused on healthcare, lower taxes, and safer communities; the Canadian Bar Association's Newfoundland and Labrador branch submitted a pre-budget recommendation calling for removal of the provincial Financial Corporations Capital Tax and improvements to the provincial tax structure.7

provinces.name: Yukon
provinces.analysis:
Province-specific GDP and unemployment figures for Yukon are not available in the current StatCan release cycle. In the national context, Mining and Oil & Gas GDP (NAICS 21) contracted 0.9% month-over-month in the latest reporting period while expanding 1.3% year-over-year; Construction GDP (NAICS 23) grew 0.3% month-over-month and 2.0% year-over-year, sectors that carry direct weight for Yukon's resource and infrastructure economy.

Agnico Eagle Mines (NYSE, TSX: AEM) acquired a 14% equity stake in Cascadia Minerals (TSXV: CAM), with proceeds directed toward the Carmacks copper-gold project in Yukon and broader regional exploration activity.1 The two companies announced a strategic alliance focused on the identification and advancement of projects within Yukon's Stikine Terrane, an area known for copper, gold, and polymetallic mineralization.2 Gold traded at $1,445 per troy ounce and silver at $72.68 per ounce as of March 31, providing the commodity backdrop for the investment.

Representatives from all three Canadian territories, including Yukon's energy minister, reported that aging electricity infrastructure had reached a critical state requiring billions of dollars in federal investment to modernize grids and maintain continuous power supply.3 Nationally, Utilities GDP (NAICS 22) expanded 2.7% month-over-month in the latest period, the strongest month-over-month gain among all tracked national sectors. Territorial representatives characterized the infrastructure deficit as requiring immediate federal action.

The Yukon government announced an expansion of the family medicine residency program, adding new training seats and advancing plans for a permanent northern medical training program to address physician availability in the territory.4 The Yukon Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources faced legislative challenges on March 28 regarding the territory's mining revenue policy.5

The federal Impact Assessment Agency recorded a status change for the Active Transportation Enhancements project at Takhini River Bridge and Klondike Highway Pavement Markings in Whitehorse, advancing the file from On Hold to Suspended.6 The project encompasses cantilevered pathways at the Takhini River Bridge and pavement markings along the Klondike Highway within the City of Whitehorse.
provinces.sectorHighlights:
National Mining and Oil & Gas GDP (NAICS 21) contracted 0.9% month-over-month while expanding 1.3% year-over-year in the latest reporting period. In Yukon's mining sector, Agnico Eagle Mines acquired a 14% stake in Cascadia Minerals to advance the Carmacks copper-gold project and expand exploration within the Stikine Terrane.12 Gold at $1,445/oz and silver at $72.68/oz represent the current commodity benchmarks relevant to the project's economics.

National Utilities GDP (NAICS 22) posted a 2.7% month-over-month gain, the strongest sectoral increase in the national accounts for the latest period. Yukon's energy minister, alongside counterparts from the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, identified aging territorial electricity grids as requiring billions in federal infrastructure investment to reach a functional standard.3 The territory's electricity infrastructure includes aging hydroelectric facilities supplemented by diesel generation across remote communities.

National Construction GDP (NAICS 23) expanded 0.3% month-over-month and 2.0% year-over-year. The Active Transportation Enhancements project at Takhini River Bridge and Klondike Highway Pavement Markings in Whitehorse, subject to federal impact assessment, recorded a status change from On Hold to Suspended in the current review cycle.6
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Province-specific unemployment, employment rate, and participation rate data for Yukon are not published on a monthly basis through StatCan's Labour Force Survey, which focuses on Census Metropolitan Areas and provinces rather than the territories individually. The healthcare sector registered a labour-side development: the Yukon government announced expansion of the family medicine residency program, adding training seats and advancing a permanent northern medical training program to address physician availability across the territory.4

Infrastructure maintenance employment on Yukon's highway network remains active, with operator roles posted for the Alaska Highway corridor near the Yukon border.7 No territory-specific wage data, youth employment figures, or participation rate trends were available in Yukon-specific sources for this reporting period.
provinces.consumerPulse: Yukon's energy minister highlighted deteriorating electricity infrastructure as a pressing consumer and community concern, noting that aging grids require billions in federal funding to maintain reliable power supply to residents and businesses.3 Energy reliability for households remains a direct consumer issue in a territory where diesel backup generation supplements hydroelectric capacity, with cost implications tied to diesel fuel prices. The Yukon government's expansion of the family medicine residency program addresses a persistent access gap in healthcare services that affects residents across the territory.4
provinces.tradeExposure:
Yukon's private sector economy is anchored by mining, with gold, silver, and zinc as the territory's primary export commodities. Gold traded at $1,445 per troy ounce and silver at $72.68 per ounce as of March 31, 2026. Agnico Eagle's acquisition of a 14% stake in Cascadia Minerals to advance the Carmacks copper-gold project represents a direct link between current commodity prices and capital deployment decisions in the territory.12

Federal transfers represent a significant component of Yukon's fiscal base, alongside seasonal tourism revenue associated with Klondike heritage and outdoor recreation. Zinc prices, the third of Yukon's key export commodities, were not available in current market feeds. The territory's trade exposure is concentrated in a small number of active and proposed mining projects, with commodity price movements carrying outsized influence on the private investment climate.
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada policy rate stands at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026. For Yukon's capital-intensive mining sector, the current rate environment determines project financing costs for developments such as the Carmacks copper-gold project. Federal infrastructure investments in the territory's electricity grid, cited by territorial ministers as requiring billions in spending, are primarily financed through federal transfers and grants rather than private capital markets, limiting direct rate sensitivity for those initiatives.3

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut-specific GDP and employment data are not available in the current StatCan provincial series. National mining and oil and gas GDP posted a 0.9% month-over-month contraction and a 1.3% year-over-year gain in the latest reading — the national benchmark for the sector anchoring Nunavut's private economy.4 The federal government completed construction of a new small craft harbour in Clyde River, and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson travelled to Iqaluit to announce additional federal marine infrastructure investments in Canada's high Arctic.23

B2Gold (TSX: BTO; NYSE-A: BTG) reported that infill drilling at the Goose area within the Back River gold district reinforces expansion potential and improves the probability of extended mine life at Nunavut's most active gold operation.4 Gold was priced at $1,445 per troy ounce as of March 31, 2026.4

The Government of Canada and the Qikiqtani Inuit Association marked the establishment of the Qikiqtait and Sarvarjuaq Marine Protected Areas in Nunavut on March 28, 2026, advancing Canada's commitment to protecting 30 per cent of the ocean by 2030.1 The federal government rejected requests from Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. for a five-year extension on the assault-style weapons ban, a regulatory decision affecting Inuit hunting practices in the territory.7

The completed Clyde River small craft harbour represents new community marine infrastructure that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans describes as enhancing safety, improving marine access, and contributing to Arctic sovereignty objectives.2 B2Gold's ongoing infill and expansion drilling program at the Goose area is focused on defining additional mineral resources within the Back River district.5
provinces.sectorHighlights:
National mining and oil and gas GDP contracted 0.9% month-over-month while recording a 1.3% year-over-year gain in the latest StatCan data. B2Gold's infill drilling campaign at the Goose area of Nunavut's Back River gold district reported results reinforcing expansion potential and the prospect of extended mine life, with exploration described as a cornerstone of B2Gold's strategy at the site.45

Federal investment in Nunavut's marine infrastructure sector advanced this week with the completion of a new small craft harbour in Clyde River and a ministerial announcement from Iqaluit signalling further investments in Arctic small craft harbours.23 The concurrent designation of the Qikiqtait and Sarvarjuaq Marine Protected Areas represents a regulatory development affecting the territory's coastal and marine environment, co-administered with the Qikiqtani Inuit Association.1
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Province-specific participation rate, employment rate, and unemployment data are not available in the current StatCan monthly series for Nunavut. The Baffinland Mary River iron ore mine and B2Gold's Back River gold project are among the territory's largest private-sector employers; their operational scale directly shapes territory-wide employment conditions.4

No specific hiring, layoff, or wage data for Nunavut was reported in available sources this week. The territory's labour market is structurally characterized by a significant public-sector presence, geographic isolation constraining workforce mobility, and federal transfer dependency that underpins public employment.
provinces.consumerPulse: An Iqaluit grocery store was broken into twice within a short period, with the RCMP appealing to the public for assistance in identifying suspects, highlighting retail security conditions in the territory's largest community.6 No specific food pricing, energy cost, or housing affordability data for Nunavut was reported in available sources this week.
provinces.tradeExposure: Gold was priced at $1,445 per troy ounce as of March 31, 2026, the primary commodity benchmark for B2Gold's Back River gold project — Nunavut's most active mining operation with active infill drilling underway.45 The Baffinland Mary River iron ore mine is the territory's largest employer and primary goods-trade generator; no iron ore price data was available in this week's reporting. Federal transfers remain the dominant fiscal input to Nunavut's economy, limiting direct commodity price exposure relative to resource-intensive provinces.
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada policy rate stood at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026. Nunavut's capital project financing draws predominantly on federal transfers and program spending rather than commercial credit markets, limiting the direct transmission of BoC rate movements to territory-level project costs. Changes in federal borrowing costs over time may affect the scale and pace of federal infrastructure commitments, including small craft harbour investments and Arctic sovereignty spending.23
